title: Deployments, Rollouts & Rollbacks
summary: How a Deployment drives ReplicaSets and Pods, and how to update, roll back, pause and scale it.

blocks.text: A Deployment is the usual way to run a **stateless** workload. You declare the desired state; the Deployment controller moves the cluster towards it at a controlled pace by creating and scaling **ReplicaSets**, which in turn create the Pods.

steps.text: A **Deployment** declares the desired state: a Pod template and a number of replicas.
It creates a **ReplicaSet**, which keeps that many Pods running and replaces any that fail.
Changing the Pod template, for example the image, creates a **new ReplicaSet**. A RollingUpdate scales it up while the old one scales down.
The old ReplicaSet is kept with 0 replicas, so `kubectl rollout undo` can return to it.

blocks.text:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: <name>
spec:
  replicas: 3            # optional, defaults to 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: <label>       # must match the template labels
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: <label>
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: <container>
        image: <image>:<tag>

items: `.spec.template` and `.spec.selector` are the only **required** fields of `.spec`.
The selector must match `.spec.template.metadata.labels` or the API rejects it. In `apps/v1` the selector is **immutable** once created.
The template's `restartPolicy` may only be `Always` (the default).
ReplicaSets are named `<deployment-name>-<hash>`. The hash is the `pod-template-hash` label the controller adds to each ReplicaSet and its Pods. Never change that label.
Don't manage ReplicaSets that a Deployment owns, and don't let other controllers or bare Pods share its selector. Kubernetes won't stop the overlap, and the controllers will fight.

blocks.text:
kubectl get deployments          # READY / UP-TO-DATE / AVAILABLE
kubectl get rs                   # DESIRED / CURRENT / READY
kubectl get pods --show-labels   # shows pod-template-hash

A ReplicaSet keeps a fixed number of identical Pods running. It has a **selector**, a **replica count** and a **Pod template**, and it creates or deletes Pods to hit the count. Each Pod points back to its ReplicaSet through `metadata.ownerReferences`.

items: Pods that are deleted or lost (for example, a node fails) are **replaced**. Bare Pods are not, so the docs recommend a ReplicaSet even for a single Pod.
A ReplicaSet **adopts** any Pod with no controller owner whose labels match its selector, even one it didn't create. Extra Pods are then terminated if the count is exceeded.
Changing a Pod's labels so they no longer match removes it from the ReplicaSet (useful for debugging); a replacement is created.
ReplicaSets don't do rolling updates. Use a Deployment unless you need custom update orchestration or no updates at all.
`kubectl delete` with `--cascade=orphan` removes only the ReplicaSet and leaves its Pods running.

blocks.text: On scale-down, Pending/unschedulable Pods go first, then Pods with a lower `controller.kubernetes.io/pod-deletion-cost` annotation, then Pods on nodes running more replicas, then newer Pods.
A rollout (and a new revision) happens **only** when `.spec.template` changes, such as an image or template label. Scaling does not trigger a rollout.

rows: New ReplicaSet scales up while the old one scales down, within maxSurge / maxUnavailable
All old Pods are killed, and their removal awaited, before any new Pod is created (downtime)
Max Pods unavailable during the update; % rounds **down**
Max Pods above the desired count; % rounds **up**

items: Values can be an absolute number or a percentage. They can't **both** be 0.
With the defaults and 3 replicas, at least 3 Pods stay available and at most 4 exist. With 4 replicas, the Pod count stays between 3 and 5.
`.spec.minReadySeconds` (default 0) is how long a new Pod must be ready without crashing before it counts as available.
If you update during an in-flight rollout, the controller starts a new ReplicaSet straight away and treats the half-scaled one as old (a **rollover**).

blocks.text:
kubectl set image deployment/<name> <container>=<image>:<tag>
kubectl edit deployment/<name>        # or edit .spec.template directly
kubectl rollout status deployment/<name>
kubectl describe deployment <name>    # events show RS scaled up/down
`kubectl rollout status` exits **0** when the rollout succeeds and **non-zero** (1) when the Deployment has exceeded its progress deadline. Handy for scripted checks.

items: `.spec.progressDeadlineSeconds` (default **600**) sets how long the controller waits before reporting the rollout as stalled: condition `Progressing`, status `False`, reason `ProgressDeadlineExceeded`. It must be greater than `minReadySeconds`.
Kubernetes only reports a stalled rollout; it does **not** roll back automatically.
Common causes of a stuck rollout: insufficient quota, failing readiness probes, image pull errors, insufficient permissions, limit ranges, app misconfiguration.
A finished rollout shows `Progressing` True with reason `NewReplicaSetAvailable`.

blocks.text:
kubectl rollout history deployment/<name>
kubectl rollout history deployment/<name> --revision=<n>
kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name>                    # previous revision
kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name> --to-revision=<n>
kubectl annotate deployment/<name> kubernetes.io/change-cause="<message>"

items: The CHANGE-CAUSE column is copied from the `kubernetes.io/change-cause` annotation. The old `--record` flag is deprecated.
Only the **Pod template** is rolled back. Replica count is not part of a revision.
Revisions live in the old ReplicaSets. `.spec.revisionHistoryLimit` (default **10**) controls how many are kept. Setting it to **0** removes them all, so you can't roll back.
You can't roll back a **paused** Deployment until you resume it.

blocks.text: Pause a Deployment to batch several template changes into **one** rollout. While paused, template edits don't start a rollout and the progress deadline isn't checked.

kubectl rollout pause deployment/<name>
kubectl set image deployment/<name> <container>=<image>:<tag>
kubectl set resources deployment/<name> -c=<container> --limits=cpu=<cpu>,memory=<memory>
kubectl rollout resume deployment/<name>

kubectl scale deployment/<name> --replicas=<n>

items: A later `kubectl apply` of a manifest overwrites a manual `kubectl scale`.
If an HPA manages the Deployment, leave `.spec.replicas` out of the manifest and let the control plane own it.
Scaling mid-rollout spreads extra replicas across the active ReplicaSets in proportion to their size (**proportional scaling**).

questions.stem: You need to update container `web` in Deployment `shop` to a new image tag. Which command starts the rolling update?

options.explanation: set image changes the Pod template, which triggers a rollout.
Scaling changes the replica count and does not trigger a rollout.
resume only continues a paused Deployment; it doesn't change the image.
undo goes back to the previous revision.

questions.stem: True or false: Running `kubectl scale` on a Deployment creates a new revision in its rollout history.

options.explanation: Revisions are created only when .spec.template changes.
Scaling doesn't create a revision, so rollbacks restore only the Pod template.

questions.stem: A Deployment has 4 replicas and the default rolling update settings. During an update, what range of Pod counts does the controller keep?

options.explanation: 25% max unavailable and 25% max surge give at least 3 available and at most 5.
maxSurge and maxUnavailable both allow some movement.
That describes no limits at all; the defaults are 25%.
The default maxSurge lets the count go above 4.

questions.stem: Your app can't run two versions side by side, so every old Pod must be gone before new ones start. Which strategy fits?

options.explanation: Recreate kills existing Pods and waits for their removal before creating new ones.
That adds a new Pod while old ones still run.

options.text: strategy.type: RollingUpdate with maxUnavailable: 0 and maxSurge: 0
options.explanation: The two values can't both be 0.
Pausing stops rollouts; it isn't an update strategy.

questions.stem: A typo in the image tag leaves new Pods in ImagePullBackOff. How do you return to the version that worked just before?

options.explanation: undo with no revision rolls back to the previous one.
Pausing stops further rollouts but doesn't restore the old template.
history lists revisions; it doesn't change anything.
That only watches the rollout; it doesn't change anything.

questions.stem: Which statements about Deployment rollout history are correct? Select 2.

options.text: Revisions are stored in the Deployment's old ReplicaSets
options.explanation: Each revision's configuration lives in its ReplicaSet.
By default 10 old ReplicaSets are kept.

options.text: Setting revisionHistoryLimit to 0 keeps unlimited history
options.explanation: 0 cleans up all old ReplicaSets, so rollback is impossible.

options.text: --record is the recommended way to fill CHANGE-CAUSE
options.explanation: --record is deprecated; set the kubernetes.io/change-cause annotation instead.

questions.stem: You want to change the image and the resource limits of a Deployment but trigger only one rollout. What's the documented approach?

options.text: kubectl rollout pause, make both changes, then kubectl rollout resume
options.explanation: Changes made while paused are rolled out together after resume.
Each template change would still trigger its own rollout.
Scaling doesn't stop template changes from starting rollouts.

options.text: Use kubectl rollout undo between the changes
options.explanation: undo reverts a change; it doesn't batch them.

questions.stem: True or false: When a Deployment exceeds its progress deadline, Kubernetes automatically rolls it back.

options.explanation: It only sets a ProgressDeadlineExceeded condition.
Higher-level tooling (or you) must act on the condition, for example by rolling back.

questions.stem: A script runs `kubectl rollout status deployment/<name>` after a rollout that stalled past its progress deadline. What does it see?

options.text: An error that the progress deadline was exceeded, and a non-zero exit code
options.explanation: rollout status returns non-zero (1) once the deadline is exceeded.
That's what a completed rollout returns.

options.text: It waits forever with no exit
options.explanation: It exits with an error once the deadline is exceeded.

options.text: The rollout is automatically undone and it exits 0
options.explanation: Kubernetes doesn't roll back on its own.

questions.stem: A node running one of a ReplicaSet's Pods fails. What happens?

options.text: The ReplicaSet creates a replacement Pod to restore the replica count
options.explanation: ReplicaSets replace Pods that are deleted or terminated, including after node failure.

options.text: Nothing; Pods are only replaced if created as bare Pods
options.explanation: It's the other way round: bare Pods are not replaced.

options.text: The ReplicaSet lowers its replica count
options.explanation: The desired count doesn't change; the controller works to meet it.

options.text: The Deployment starts a new revision
options.explanation: Only Pod template changes create revisions.

questions.stem: A ReplicaSet with selector `tier: frontend` already runs its 3 desired Pods. You then create a bare Pod labelled `tier: frontend`. What happens to it?

options.text: The ReplicaSet adopts it and then terminates it, because it now has too many Pods
options.explanation: Matching Pods without a controller owner are acquired, and the excess is deleted.

options.text: It runs alongside the 3 Pods, unmanaged
options.explanation: A ReplicaSet acquires matching Pods that have no controller owner.
Kubernetes doesn't block overlapping labels.
.spec.replicas doesn't change.

questions.stem: Which statements about a Deployment's spec are correct? Select 3.

options.explanation: Otherwise the API rejects the Deployment.

options.text: In apps/v1, .spec.selector can't be changed after creation
options.explanation: To change it, delete and recreate the Deployment.
It's optional and defaults to 1.

options.text: The Pod template may use restartPolicy: OnFailure
options.explanation: Only Always is allowed in a Deployment template.

questions.stem: You ran `kubectl scale deployment/<name> --replicas=8`, then `kubectl apply -f` the original manifest, which has `replicas: 3`. How many replicas are desired now?

options.text: 3, because applying the manifest overwrites the manual scaling
options.explanation: The docs warn that apply overwrites an earlier manual scale.
The applied manifest's replicas value replaces it.
Replica counts are not summed.

options.text: The apply fails with a conflict
options.explanation: The apply succeeds and sets replicas to 3.

questions.stem: You paused a Deployment and now want to run `kubectl rollout undo`. What must you do first?

options.text: Resume it with kubectl rollout resume
options.explanation: A paused Deployment can't be rolled back until it's resumed.
Scaling doesn't unpause it.
That deletes the history you need to roll back.
The docs say you can't roll back while paused.
